      "id": "ie402_desc",
      "t": "This course introduces students to the principles and practices of systems engineering, focusing on the analysis,\ndesign, and management of complex systems. Through a blend of theoretical concepts and practical applications, students\nlearn   how   to   approach   and   solve   large-scale   engineering   problems   involving   multiple   components,   stakeholders,   and\noperational constraints. Key topics include requirements analysis, systems design, integration, project management, and\nperformance evaluation. \nStudents will develop skills in modeling and optimizing systems that integrate people, processes, and technology. They\nwill explore methods for ensuring that systems are efficient, reliable, and adaptable across various industries, such as\nmanufacturing, healthcare, and logistics. This course prepares BSIE students to play a vital role in creating systems that\nmaximize performance, minimize waste, and support organizational goals. \nBeyond   technical   knowledge,   the   course   integrates   Marian   Augustinian   values   into   each   lesson,   fostering   the\ndevelopment of students as Christo-centric Catholic professionals. The curriculum not only aims for intellectual growth but also\ninstills a commitment to ethical decision-making, social responsibility, and compassionate service. Week 2-3 course content: Introduction to
Systems Engineering
• Introduction to
Systems
Engineering
Management
• Systems
Engineering
Management in
DoD Acquisition
ILOs:
- ILO1: Describe fundamental principles of systems engineering, including system life cycles, requirements analysis, and systems thinking. [CLO 1], [CLO 2]
- ILO2: Develop basic system designs that incorporate requirements from multiple disciplines, including human factors, technology, and organizational needs. [CLO 1], [CLO 2]

Target

Lecture and Case Study
Analysis
Activity: Present a
lecture on the basics of
systems engineering
management, followed by
an analysis of a real-
world case study in
systems engineering,
such as a notable DoD
acquisition project.
Interactive Discussion
and Q&A
Activity: Facilitate an
interactive class
discussion on the key
principles of systems
engineering management
and its importance in
large-scale projects,
especially in high-stakes
environments like
defense.

Week 5-8 course content: The Systems
Engineering Process
• Systems
Engineering
Process Overview
• Requirements
Analysis
• Functional
Analysis and
Allocation
• Design Synthesis
• Verification
• Systems
Engineering
Process Outputs
ILOs:
- ILO3: Summarize the overall systems engineering process, explaining each phase from requirements analysis to verification and process outputs. [CLO1][CLO2]
- ILO4: Analyze and define system requirements based on stakeholder needs, constraints, and project objectives. [CLO2][CLO3]
- ILO5: Recognize key outputs of the systems engineering process, such as documentation, specifications, and test reports, and evaluate their role in supporting successful project outcomes. [CLO2][CLO3]

Target

Group Workshop on
Functional Analysis
and Allocation
Activity: In small groups,
students will break down
system requirements into
functional components
and allocate these to
hypothetical subsystems.
Group Workshop on
Functional Analysis
and Allocation
In small groups, students
will break down system
requirements into
functional components
and allocate these to
hypothetical subsystems.
Reflection Assignment
on Process Outputs
Have students reflect on
the outputs generated at
each stage of the
systems engineering
process and discuss how
these support project
success.

BM1-IE402-120 · Activity-fit

verified-syllabus · IE-402 · Systems Engineering · academic-semantic

Source

Week 10-11 course content: Systems Analysis
and Control
• Work
Breakdown
Structure
• Configuration
Management
• Technical
Reviews and
Audits
• Trade Studies
• Modeling and
Simulation
• Metrics
• Risk
Management
ILOs:
- ILO6: Create and interpret a WBS to organize and manage project components, identifying key deliverables and tasks for effective project planning and control. [CLO 3] [CLO4]
- ILO7: Apply modeling and simulation techniques to analyze system behavior, test potential solutions, and predict outcomes in a controlled virtual environment. [CLO 3] [CLO4]
- ILO8:Identify, assess, and manage risks within a systems project, developing risk mitigation strategies to minimize potential negative impacts on project outcomes. [CLO 3] [CLO4]

Target

Interactive Workshop
on Work Breakdown
Structure (WBS)
Creation
Activity: Conduct an
interactive workshop
where students create a
WBS for a hypothetical
project, breaking down
tasks and identifying
deliverables.
Case Study on
Configuration
Management
Activity: Present a case
study demonstrating
configuration
management principles
and practices in a real-
world project. Have
students discuss the role
of configuration
management in
maintaining system
consistency.
Risk Management
Analysis Activity
Activity: Present a
project scenario and ask
students to identify
potential risks, assess
their impact and
probability, and develop
mitigation strategies.

Source

Week 12-14 course content: Planning, Organizing
and Managing
• Systems
Engineering
Planning
• Product
Improvement
Strategies
• Organizing and
Integrating
System
Development
• Contractual
Considerations
• Management
Considerations
and Summary
ILOs:
- ILO9: Formulate a comprehensive systems engineering plan that outlines objectives, resources, timelines, and milestones to guide system development from inception through completion. [CLO 3] [CLO4]
- ILO10: Evaluate essential management considerations—such as resource allocation, risk assessment, and stakeholder engagement—and their impact on project success, applying these principles to real or simulated project scenarios. [CLO 3] [CLO4]

Target

Workshop on Systems
Engineering Planning
Conduct a hands-on
workshop where students
outline a systems
engineering plan for a
hypothetical project. They
should include project
objectives, resource
allocation, timeline
planning, and key
milestones.
Product Improvement
Strategy Brainstorming
Session
In groups, students
brainstorm and propose
strategies for iterative
product improvement in a
given scenario, focusing
on design, functionality,
and customer feedback
loops.

      "id": "ie402_desc",
      "t": "This course introduces students to the principles and practices of systems engineering, focusing on the analysis,\ndesign, and management of complex systems. Through a blend of theoretical concepts and practical applications, students\nlearn   how   to   approach   and   solve   large-scale   engineering   problems   involving   multiple   components,   stakeholders,   and\noperational constraints. Key topics include requirements analysis, systems design, integration, project management, and\nperformance evaluation. \nStudents will develop skills in modeling and optimizing systems that integrate people, processes, and technology. They\nwill explore methods for ensuring that systems are efficient, reliable, and adaptable across various industries, such as\nmanufacturing, healthcare, and logistics. This course prepares BSIE students to play a vital role in creating systems that\nmaximize performance, minimize waste, and support organizational goals. \nBeyond   technical   knowledge,   the   course   integrates   Marian   Augustinian   values   into   each   lesson,   fostering   the\ndevelopment of students as Christo-centric Catholic professionals. The curriculum not only aims for intellectual growth but also\ninstills a commitment to ethical decision-making, social responsibility, and compassionate service. Students will be equipped\nwith the knowledge and values necessary to thrive as professionals in the field of Industrial Engineering."

BM1-IE402-122 · Activity-fit

verified-syllabus · IE-402 · Systems Engineering · academic-semantic

Source

Week 15-17 course content: Application
• Systems
Engineering As
Human Activity
• Trade Space
Exploration
Concept
Selection
• Experiments
• Robust Design I
• Robust Design
II
ILOs:
- ILO11: Analyze and evaluate multiple design alternatives through trade space exploration, applying criteria to select the optimal concept based on performance, feasibility, and stakeholder needs. [CLO 3] [CLO4]
- ILO 12: Develop and execute experiments to validate design assumptions, analyze system behaviors, and refine solutions, demonstrating an understanding of experimental design and data collection principles. [CLO 3] [CLO4]
- ILO 13: Identify critical factors in system design that influence performance consistency, and apply robust design techniques to improve reliability under varying conditions (Robust Design I). [CLO 3] [CLO4]
- ILO14: Utilize advanced robust design methods to enhance system resilience, focusing on minimizing performance variability in complex, multi-variable systems (Robust Design II). [CLO 3] [CLO4]

Target

Case Study Discussion:
Systems Engineering
as a Human Activity
Provide a case study that
highlights the role of
human factors in systems
engineering, including
team dynamics,
stakeholder involvement,
and ethical
considerations. Facilitate
a class discussion on the
human-centered aspects
and their impact on
project outcomes.
Design and Conduct
Experiments Activity
Assign students a mini-
project to design and
conduct an experiment to
validate a system
component or process.
They should identify the
objective, develop a
methodology, collect
data, and analyze results
to inform design
improvements.
Robust Design
Brainstorming Session
(Robust Design I)
In small groups, students
brainstorm how to apply
basic robust design
principles to make a
system more stable
under varying conditions.
They discuss factors that
influence system stability
and propose design
adjustments to minimize
variability.
Advanced Robust
Design Project (Robust
Design II)
Activity: For a more
complex project, students
apply advanced robust
design techniques to a
hypothetical or real-world
system. They identify and
control multiple variables
to minimize performance
variation across diverse
scenarios.

- Interiority: Interiority is the practice of turning inward, encountering our true selves, and allowing God’s presence to transform us. Through prayer, reflection, and contemplative silence, we confront our weaknesses and sinfulness, but also rediscover our dignity as children of God. This journey within leads us to an authentic relationship with Him and guides us to live with clarity and peace.

Target

• Interiority
• Respect
• Obedience

Week 2-3 course content: Introduction to
Systems Engineering
• Introduction to
Systems
Engineering
Management
• Systems
Engineering
Management in
DoD Acquisition
ILOs:
- ILO1: Describe fundamental principles of systems engineering, including system life cycles, requirements analysis, and systems thinking. [CLO 1], [CLO 2]
- ILO2: Develop basic system designs that incorporate requirements from multiple disciplines, including human factors, technology, and organizational needs. [CLO 1], [CLO 2]
Learning activities: Lecture and Case Study Analysis Activity: Present a lecture on the basics of systems engineering management, followed by an analysis of a real- world case study in systems engineering, such as a notable DoD acquisition project. Interactive Discussion and Q&A Activity: Facilitate an interactive class discussion on the key principles of systems engineering management and its importance in large-scale projects, especially in high-stakes environments like defense.
Assessment tasks: Quiz on Fundamental Concepts Conduct a quiz covering key concepts and terminology in systems engineering management, including its principles, life cycle stages, and specific applications in DoD acquisition. Case Study Analysis Report Provide a case study on a DoD acquisition project or a similar large-scale systems engineering project. Students will analyze and write a report covering the systems
Definitions of the values named (from the institution's published wording; approval status: pending_approval):
- Courage: Courage is the strength to stand firm in truth and goodness. It is the freedom to express one’s thoughts responsibly, the boldness to give and receive fraternal correction, and the integrity to choose what is right even when it is difficult or unpopular. Rooted in Gospel values, courage empowers us to live authentically and faithfully in service of God and others.
- Humility: Humility allows us to see ourselves and others through the lens of truth and grace. It teaches us to acknowledge both our strengths and limitations, to welcome correction with openness, and to use every experience as an opportunity for growth. Above all, humility reminds us to be grateful to God who created each of us uniquely for a purpose greater than ourselves.

Target

• Understanding
and patience
in
learning
• Creative and
critical thinking
• Analytical
thinking
• Good active
participation
and
involvement
• Appreciation
• Effective and
efficient
management
of resources
• Appreciation

• Courage and
Humility

- ILO5: Recognize key outputs of the systems engineering process, such as documentation, specifications, and test reports, and evaluate their role in supporting successful project outcomes. [CLO2][CLO3]

  "description": [
    {
      "id": "ie402_desc",
      "t": "This course introduces students to the principles and practices of systems engineering, focusing on the analysis,\ndesign, and management of complex systems. Through a blend of theoretical concepts and practical applications, students\nlearn   how   to   approach   and   solve   large-scale   engineering   problems   involving   multiple   components,   stakeholders,   and\noperational constraints. Key topics include requirements analysis, systems design, integration, project management, and\nperformance evaluation. \nStudents will develop skills in modeling and optimizing systems that integrate people, processes, and technology. They\nwill explore methods for ensuring that systems are efficient, reliable, and adaptable across various industries, such as\nmanufacturing, healthcare, and logistics. This course prepares BSIE students to play a vital role in creating systems that\nmaximize performance, minimize waste, and support organizational goals. \nBeyond   technical   knowledge,   the   course   integrates   Marian   Augustinian   values   into   each   lesson,   fostering   the\ndevelopment of students as Christo-centric Catholic professionals. The curriculum not only aims for intellectual growth but also\ninstills a commitment to ethical decision-making, social responsibility, and compassionate service. Students will be equipped\nwith the knowledge and values necessary to thrive as professionals in the field of Industrial Engineering."
    }
  ],

Source

Week 10-11 course content: Systems Analysis
and Control
• Work
Breakdown
Structure
• Configuration
Management
• Technical
Reviews and
Audits
• Trade Studies
• Modeling and
Simulation
• Metrics
• Risk
Management
ILOs:
- ILO6: Create and interpret a WBS to organize and manage project components, identifying key deliverables and tasks for effective project planning and control. [CLO 3] [CLO4]
- ILO7: Apply modeling and simulation techniques to analyze system behavior, test potential solutions, and predict outcomes in a controlled virtual environment. [CLO 3] [CLO4]
- ILO8:Identify, assess, and manage risks within a systems project, developing risk mitigation strategies to minimize potential negative impacts on project outcomes. [CLO 3] [CLO4]
Learning activities: Interactive Workshop on Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) Creation Activity: Conduct an interactive workshop where students create a WBS for a hypothetical project, breaking down tasks and identifying deliverables. Case Study on Configuration Management Activity: Present a case study demonstrating configuration management principles and practices in a real- world project. Have students discuss the role of configuration management in maintaining system consistency. Risk Management Analysis Activity 
Assessment tasks: Peer Review of Experimental Design and Robustness Plan Ask students to peer review each other’s experimental design proposals and robustness plans, providing constructive feedback on methodology and approach. Risk Assessment and Mitigation in Robust Design Assign a task where students assess potential risks to robustness in a system design and develop mitigation strategies to address these risks.
No institutional definition of the values named is supplied: judge only what the lesson text itself shows.

Target

• Understanding
and patience
in learning
• Creative and
critical thinking
• Analytical
thinking
• Good and
active
participation
and
involvement
• Appreciation
• Effective and
efficient
management
of resources
• Problem
solving skills

ILOs:
- ILO9: Formulate a comprehensive systems engineering plan that outlines objectives, resources, timelines, and milestones to guide system development from inception through completion. [CLO 3] [CLO4]
- ILO10: Evaluate essential management considerations—such as resource allocation, risk assessment, and stakeholder engagement—and their impact on project success, applying these principles to real or simulated project scenarios. [CLO 3] [CLO4]
Learning activities: Workshop on Systems Engineering Planning Conduct a hands-on workshop where students outline a systems engineering plan for a hypothetical project. They should include project objectives, resource allocation, timeline planning, and key milestones. Product Improvement Strategy Brainstorming Session In groups, students brainstorm and propose strategies for iterative product improvement in a given scenario, focusing on design, functionality, and customer feedback loops.
Assessment tasks: Systems Engineering Plan Development Task: Have students create a comprehensive systems engineering plan for a hypothetical project. This plan should include objectives, resource allocation, timeline, milestones, risk assessment, and project phases. Concept

ILOs:
- ILO11: Analyze and evaluate multiple design alternatives through trade space exploration, applying criteria to select the optimal concept based on performance, feasibility, and stakeholder needs. [CLO 3] [CLO4]
- ILO 12: Develop and execute experiments to validate design assumptions, analyze system behaviors, and refine solutions, demonstrating an understanding of experimental design and data collection principles. [CLO 3] [CLO4]
- ILO 13: Identify critical factors in system design that influence performance consistency, and apply robust design techniques to improve reliability under varying conditions (Robust Design I). [CLO 3] [CLO4]
- ILO14: Utilize advanced robust design methods to enhance system resilience, focusing on minimizing performance variability in complex, multi-variable systems (Robust Design II). [CLO 3] [CLO4]
Learning activities: Case Study Discussion: Systems Engineering as a Human Activity Provide a case study that highlights the role of human factors in systems engineering, including team dynamics, stakeholder involvement, and ethical considerations. BM1-IE402-129 · Title-description

verified-syllabus · IE-402 · Systems Engineering · academic-semantic

Source

Course title: Systems Engineering
Course code: IE-402
Program: BSIE

Target

This course introduces students to the principles and practices of systems engineering, focusing on the analysis,
design, and management of complex systems. Through a blend of theoretical concepts and practical applications, students
learn   how   to   approach   and   solve   large-scale   engineering   problems   involving   multiple   components,   stakeholders,   and
operational constraints. Key topics include requirements analysis, systems design, integration, project management, and
performance evaluation. 
Students will develop skills in modeling and optimizing systems that integrate people, processes, and technology. They
will explore methods for ensuring that systems are efficient, reliable, and adaptable across various industries, such as
manufacturing, healthcare, and logistics. This course prepares BSIE students to play a vital role in creating systems that
maximize performance, minimize waste, and support organizational goals. 
Beyond   technical   knowledge,   the   course   integrates   Marian   Augustinian   values   into   each   lesson,   fostering   the
development of students as Christo-centric Catholic professionals. The curriculum not only aims for intellectual growth but also
instills a commitment to ethical decision-making, social responsibility, and compassionate service. Students will be equipped
with the knowledge and values necessary to thrive as professionals in the field of Industrial Engineering.

BM1-IE402-130 · Week1-introduction

verified-syllabus · IE-402 · Systems Engineering · academic-semantic

Source

Course title: Systems Engineering
Course code: IE-402
Program: BSIE
Course objectives (CLOs):
CLO 1: Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of engineering and management principles by effectively leading and collaborating within teams, managing projects, and engaging in multidisciplinary environments.
CLO 2: Apply critical and creative thinking skills to analyze, design, and optimize complex systems, integrating various components such as people, materials, technology, and information.
CLO 3: Develop the ability to identify and solve systems engineering challenges, making decisions that improve performance, enhance efficiency, and support sustainable practices across diverse industries.
CLO 4: Demonstrate the Filipino- Catholic Augustinian Spirituality through value webbing.

Week 2-3 course content: Introduction to
Systems Engineering
• Introduction to
Systems
Engineering
Management
• Systems
Engineering
Management in
DoD Acquisition
ILOs:
- ILO1: Describe fundamental principles of systems engineering, including system life cycles, requirements analysis, and systems thinking. [CLO 1], [CLO 2]
- ILO2: Develop basic system designs that incorporate requirements from multiple disciplines, including human factors, technology, and organizational needs. [CLO 1], [CLO 2]
Learning activities: Lecture and Case Study Analysis Activity: Present a lecture on the basics of systems engineering management, followed by an analysis of a real- world case study in systems engineering, such as a notable DoD acquisition project. Interactive Discussion and Q&A Activity: Facilitate an interactive class discussion on the key principles of systems engineering management and its importance in large-scal

Target

Quiz on
Fundamental
Concepts
Conduct a quiz
covering key concepts
and terminology in
systems engineering
management,
including its
principles, life cycle
stages, and specific
applications in DoD
acquisition.
Case Study Analysis
Report
Provide a case study
on a DoD acquisition
project or a similar
large-scale systems
engineering project.
Students will analyze
and write a report
covering the systems
engineering
management
challenges and
solutions highlighted
in the case.

      "t": "This course introduces students to the principles and practices of systems engineering, focusing on the analysis,\ndesign, and management of complex systems. Through a blend of theoretical concepts and practical applications, students\nlearn   how   to   approach   and   solve   large-scale   engineering   problems   involving   multiple   components,   stakeholders,   and\noperational constraints. Key topics include requirements analysis, systems design, integration, project management, and\nperformance evaluation. \nStudents will develop skills in modeling and optimizing systems that integrate people, processes, and technology. They\nwill explore methods for ensuring that systems are efficient, reliable, and adaptable across various industries, such as\nmanufacturing, healthcare, and logistics. This course prepares BSIE students to play a vital role in creating systems that\nmaximize performance, minimize waste, and support organizational goals. \nBeyond   technical   knowledge,   the   course   integrates   Marian   Augustinian   values   into   each   lesson,   fostering   the\ndevelopment of students as Christo-centric Catholic professionals. - ILO10: Evaluate essential management considerations—such as resource allocation, risk assessment, and stakeholder engagement—and their impact on project success, applying these principles to real or simulated project scenarios. [CLO 3] [CLO4]

Through a blend of theoretical concepts and practical applications, students\nlearn   how   to   approach   and   solve   large-scale   engineering   problems   involving   multiple   components,   stakeholders,   and\noperational constraints. Key topics include requirements analysis, systems design, integration, project management, and\nperformance evaluation. \nStudents will develop skills in modeling and optimizing systems that integrate people, processes, and technology. They\nwill explore methods for ensuring that systems are efficient, reliable, and adaptable across various industries, such as\nmanufacturing, healthcare, and logistics. This course prepares BSIE students to play a vital role in creating systems that\nmaximize performance, minimize waste, and support organizational goals. \nBeyond   technical   knowledge,   the   course   integrates   Marian   Augustinian   values   into   each   lesson,   fostering   the\ndevelopment of students as Christo-centric Catholic professionals. The curriculum not only aims for intellectual growth but also\ninstills a commitment to ethical decision-making, social responsibility, and compassionate service. Students will be equipped\nwith the knowledge and values necessary to thrive as professionals in the field of Industrial Engineering."
    }
  ],

Week 15-17 course content: Application
• Systems
Engineering As
Human Activity
• Trade Space
Exploration
Concept
Selection
• Experiments
• Robust Design I
• Robust Design
II
ILOs:
- ILO11: Analyze and evaluate multiple design alternatives through trade space exploration, applying criteria to select the optimal concept based on performance, feasibility, and stakeholder needs. [CLO 3] [CLO4]
- ILO 12: Develop and execute experiments to validate design assumptions, analyze system behaviors, and refine solutions, demonstrating an understanding of experimental design and data collection principles. [CLO 3] [CLO4]
- ILO 13: Identify critical factors in system design that influence performance consistency, and apply robust design techniques to improve reliability under varying conditions (Robust Design I). [CLO 3] [CLO4]
- ILO14: Utilize advanced robust design methods to enhance system resilience, focusing on minimizing performance variability in complex, multi-variable systems (Robust Design II). [CLO 3] [CLO4]
Learning activities: Case Study Discussion: Systems Engineering as a Human Activity Provide a case study that highlights the role of human factors in systems engineering, including team dynamics, stakeholder involvement, and ethical considerations. Facilitate a class discussion on the human-centered aspects and their impact on project outcomes. Design and Conduct Experiments Activity Assign students a mini- project to

System Evaluation
and Improvement
Proposal
Task: Have students
apply basic robust
design techniques to
evaluate a system
and propose design
changes that would

under varying
conditions. They

suggest
improvements to

Robust Design II –
Advanced Design
Analysis
Task: For a more
complex system,
students should apply
advanced robust
design methods to
assess and improve
the system’s
performance. They
will use tools such as
design of experiments
(DOE) to explore
multiple design
variables and their
interactions.
Robust Design
Report (I & II)
Task: Students will
submit a report for
each part of the
robust design
application, detailing
the steps taken to
assess and improve
system performance.
For Robust Design I,
they will focus on
basic principles, and
for Robust Design II,
they will apply
advanced techniques
to optimize the
system.

The curriculum not only aims for intellectual growth but also\ninstills a commitment to ethical decision-making, social responsibility, and compassionate service. Students will be equipped\nwith the knowledge and values necessary to thrive as professionals in the field of Industrial Engineering."
    }

  "description": [
    {
      "id": "ie402_desc",
      "t": "This course introduces students to the principles and practices of systems engineering, focusing on the analysis,\ndesign, and management of complex systems. Through a blend of theoretical concepts and practical applications, students\nlearn   how   to   approach   and   solve   large-scale   engineering   problems   involving   multiple   components,   stakeholders,   and\noperational constraints. Key topics include requirements analysis, systems design, integration, project management, and\nperformance evaluation. \nStudents will develop skills in modeling and optimizing systems that integrate people, processes, and technology. They\nwill explore methods for ensuring that systems are efficient, reliable, and adaptable across various industries, such as\nmanufacturing, healthcare, and logistics. This course prepares BSIE students to play a vital role in creating systems that\nmaximize performance, minimize waste, and support organizational goals. \nBeyond   technical   knowledge,   the   course   integrates   Marian   Augustinian   values   into   each   lesson,   fostering   the\ndevelopment of students as Christo-centric Catholic professionals. The curriculum not only aims for intellectual growth but also\ninstills a commitment to ethical decision-making, social responsibility, and compassionate service. Students will be equipped\nwith the knowledge and values necessary to thrive as professionals in the field of Industrial Engineering."
    }

  "description": [
    {
      "id": "ie402_desc",
      "t": "This course introduces students to the principles and practices of systems engineering, focusing on the analysis,\ndesign, and management of complex systems. Through a blend of theoretical concepts and practical applications, students\nlearn   how   to   approach   and   solve   large-scale   engineering   problems   involving   multiple   components,   stakeholders,   and\noperational constraints. Key topics include requirements analysis, systems design, integration, project management, and\nperformance evaluation. \nStudents will develop skills in modeling and optimizing systems that integrate people, processes, and technology. They\nwill explore methods for ensuring that systems are efficient, reliable, and adaptable across various industries, such as\nmanufacturing, healthcare, and logistics. This course prepares BSIE students to play a vital role in creating systems that\nmaximize performance, minimize waste, and support organizational goals. \nBeyond   technical   knowledge,   the   course   integrates   Marian   Augustinian   values   into   each   lesson,   fostering   the\ndevelopment of students as Christo-centric Catholic professionals. The curriculum not only aims for intellectual growth but also\ninstills a commitment to ethical decision-making, social responsibility, and compassionate service. Students will be equipped\nwith the knowledge and values necessary to thrive as professionals in the field of Industrial Engineering."
    }

{
  "meta": {

  "description": [
    {
      "id": "ie402_desc",
      "t": "This course introduces students to the principles and practices of systems engineering, focusing on the analysis,\ndesign, and management of complex systems. Through a blend of theoretical concepts and practical applications, students\nlearn   how   to   approach   and   solve   large-scale   engineering   problems   involving   multiple   components,   stakeholders,   and\noperational constraints. Key topics include requirements analysis, systems design, integration, project management, and\nperformance evaluation. \nStudents will develop skills in modeling and optimizing systems that integrate people, processes, and technology. They\nwill explore methods for ensuring that systems are efficient, reliable, and adaptable across various industries, such as\nmanufacturing, healthcare, and logistics. This course prepares BSIE students to play a vital role in creating systems that\nmaximize performance, minimize waste, and support organizational goals. \nBeyond   technical   knowledge,   the   course   integrates   Marian   Augustinian   values   into   each   lesson,   fostering   the\ndevelopment of students as Christo-centric Catholic professionals. The curriculum not only aims for intellectual growth but also\ninstills a commitment to ethical decision-making, social responsibility, and compassionate service. Students will be equipped\nwith the knowledge and values necessary to thrive as professionals in the field of Industrial Engineering."
    }

Source

Week 1 course content: Introduction to SYSTEMS ENGINEERING and the supplied course objectives
ILOs:
- Explain the course subject and the supplied course objectives.
Learning activities: Analyze a stakeholder case with guided diagrams and text descriptions, then construct a requirements matrix in groups.
Assessment tasks: Submit a requirements matrix and defend how the stated interfaces meet stakeholder needs.
Definitions of the values named (from the institution's published wording; approval status: pending_approval):
- Courage: Courage is the strength to stand firm in truth and goodness. It is the freedom to express one’s thoughts responsibly, the boldness to give and receive fraternal correction, and the integrity to choose what is right even when it is difficult or unpopular. Rooted in Gospel values, courage empowers us to live authentically and faithfully in service of God and others.

Target

Courage: explain a decision and revise it after evidence-based peer feedback.

BM1-S13-032 · Week1-introduction

synthetic · IE-402 · SYSTEMS ENGINEERING · academic-semantic

Source

Course title: SYSTEMS ENGINEERING
Course code: IE-402
Program: BSIE
Course objectives (CLOs):
CLO 1: Explain the concepts of System boundaries, stakeholder requirements and verification criteria.
CLO 2: Derive verifiable system requirements and identify interfaces for the stated engineering system.
CLO 3: Demonstrate and justify a solution involving System boundaries, stakeholder requirements and verification criteria.
CLO 4: Practice honest reporting and responsible teamwork while studying System boundaries, stakeholder requirements and verification criteria.

Target

Introduction to SYSTEMS ENGINEERING and the supplied course objectives
Explain the course subject and the supplied course objectives.
Analyze a stakeholder case with guided diagrams and text descriptions, then construct a requirements matrix in groups.
